items.title: — Carl Sagan, Pale Blue Dot, 1994
items.summary: Look again at that dot. That's here. That's home. That's us. On it everyone you love, everyone you know, everyone you ever heard of, every human being who ever was, lived out their lives.
items.body_excerpt:
Look again at that dot. That's here. That's home. That's us. On it everyone you love, everyone you know, everyone you ever heard of, every human being who ever was, lived out their lives. The aggregate of our joy and suffering, thousands of confident religions, ideologies, and economic doctrines, every hunter and forager, every hero and coward, every creator and destroyer of civilization, every king and peasant, every young couple in love, every mother and father, hopeful child, inventor and explorer, every teacher of morals, every corrupt politician, every "superstar," every "supreme leader," every saint and sinner in the history of our species lived there--on a mote of dust suspended in a sunbeam.

The Earth is a very small stage in a vast cosmic arena. Think of the rivers of blood spilled by all those generals and emperors so that, in glory and triumph, they could become the momentary masters of a fraction of a dot. Think of the endless cruelties visited by the inhabitants of one corner of this pixel on the scarcely distinguishable inhabitants of some other corner, how frequent their misunderstandings, how eager they are to kill one another, how fervent their hatreds.

Our posturings, our imagined self-importance, the delusion that we have some privileged position in the Universe, are challenged by this point of pale light. Our planet is a lonely speck in the great enveloping cosmic dark. In our obscurity, in all this vastness, there is no hint that help will come from elsewhere to save us from ourselves.

The Earth is the only world known so far to harbor life. There is nowhere else, at least in the near future, to which our species could migrate. Visit, yes. Settle, not yet. Like it or not, for the moment the Earth is where we make our stand.

It has been said that astronomy is a humbling and character-building experience. There is perhaps no better demonstration of the folly of human conceits than this distant image of our tiny world. To me, it underscores our responsibility to deal more kindly with one another, and to preserve and cherish the pale blue dot, the only home we've ever known.

— Carl Sagan, Pale Blue Dot, 1994

items.title: Today is June 14th 2023.
items.summary:
Today is June 14th 2023.
My story begins with a single droplet of rain. Time slows as the sounds fade into white noise, the droplet has seen the world from such a different view and has gone through so much in such a short amount of time.
items.body_excerpt:
Today is June 14th 2023.
My story begins with a single droplet of rain. Time slows as the sounds fade into white noise, the droplet has seen the world from such a different view and has gone through so much in such a short amount of time. forming in the clouds above and condensing into existence. Free falling toward the earth now, watching the ground get closer as a plane flies by. What a sight that must have been. Happy, excited and full of glee as new things to see come into focus. "Yay" thinks the droplet as the ground approaches. Splash.... the droplet smashes into the ocean. 
I am home now

as fr, SUBSTR(CAST(txid as varchar), 3) || 'i0' as id, * from sequenced ), cal_fd as ( select fr, count(1) as fd from cal_fr group by fr order by fd asc ), cal_point as ( select (1000-seq)+t.fr/f.fd items.body_excerpt:
Project Rooted in Bitcoin.

Constitutive Text #2: Ordinomics.

We create things on bitcoin; ordinal, inscribed text, brc20 token, and anything that the future may hold in store. Call these digital artifacts.
When we sell a digital artifact: 50% of the income will be used to fund new creations, such as by inscribing, obtaining rare sats, and commissioning new artists.

Holding a digital artifact functions as an ongoing raffle ticket for anything that we create in the future. An appropriate share of newly created artifacts will be distributed to bitcoin addresses holding older artifacts (depending in part on the type of artifact). What you obtain now, may be a little seed growing into a diverse collection (shaped by contingency and time, as the best things in life find their shape).

If we continue to sell, our funds increase, empowering us to build ever greater things, increasing the value of anything that you hold twice over: because your digital artifact increases in value and because your existing item is an ongoing raffle ticket to ever more valuable new creations.

We do not focus on directly shilling our own work. We engage with and support projects that build on bitcoin, that we think are in line with our view of the transformation of bitcoin and hyperbitcoinization, under the banner of our creations. We aim for indirect publicity for Rooted in Bitcoin by giving direct publicity to projects that we think might prove valuable and bring the space forwards. We invite others to join in this outward looking and supportive approach to our movement.

items.body_excerpt:
Project Rooted in Bitcoin.

Constitutive Text #1: Motivating View. 

This is the Summer of 2023. Bitcoin culture is changing. Bitcoin is changing.

Taproot changed what was possible with bitcoin; ordinals changed the way we use and conceptualize bitcoin. Bitcoin is constituted by both code and social uptake. With changes in code and convention comes a transformation in the very nature of bitcoin.

Code and conceptual framing need to find a natural fit. With each other, and with the wider world that bitcoin interacts with. The framing of bitcoin as a digital currency or digital asset proves to be an imperfect fit. The code does not meet the expectations set by the currency framing and the currency framing narrows the utility provided by the code, stalling development.

From being conceptualized as a digital currency and explained as such, bitcoin is now starting to become conceptualized as a layer for things to be created on. The reconceptualization fits well. The core utility that bitcoin provides is a trustless, decentralized and immutable record keeper. We are only starting to discover the many ways in which this can be used.

As block space gets used in more ways it will inevitably become more valuable. As it becomes more valuable, it becomes more expensive. With the economic incentive to minimize use of bitcoin’s block space, the market creates demand for Layer 2s (or sidechains), differing in the ways, frequency and depth with which they settle in bitcoin. This is something to embrace, and push for. Bitcoin is not sound money; but sound money will eventually be built on bitcoin, alongside many other pillars of human civilization.

A change in bitcoin implies a change in the prospect of hyperbitcoinization. No longer is this merely the prospect of bitcoin becoming the dominant global currency. Hyperbitcoinization is the prospect of different facets of humanity, from art to finance to social organization, becoming evermore deeply and widely rooted in bitcoin.

This is the conception bitcoin that is quickly changing from fringe to mainstream. This is the vision that we aim to express, document and contribute to in this project, Rooted in Bitcoin.

items.summary: We must defend our own privacy if we expect to have any. We must come together and create systems which allow anonymous transactions to take place.
items.body_excerpt: We must defend our own privacy if we expect to have any. We must come together and create systems which allow anonymous transactions to take place. People have been defending their own privacy for centuries with whispers, darkness, envelopes, closed doors, secret handshakes, and couriers. The technologies of the past did not allow for strong privacy, but electronic technologies do.

items.title: Cypherpunks write code. We know that someone has to write software to defend privacy, and since we can't get privacy unless we all do, we're going to write it. We publish our code so that our fellow Cypherpunks may practice and play with it
items.summary: Cypherpunks write code. We know that someone has to write software to defend privacy, and since we can't get privacy unless we all do, we're going to write it. We publish our code so that our fellow Cypherpunks may practice and play with it.
items.body_excerpt: Cypherpunks write code. We know that someone has to write software to defend privacy, and since we can't get privacy unless we all do, we're going to write it. We publish our code so that our fellow Cypherpunks may practice and play with it. Our code is free for all to use, worldwide. We don't much care if you don't approve of the software we write. We know that software can't be destroyed and that a widely dispersed system can't be shut down.

Manuscript

E.L. Fitzgerald

Leon Romero III was born with an intellectual curiosity and a propensity for question asking which made him undeniably his motherÕs son. He was strongly opinionated and a bit temperamental, a trait that got him in trouble growing up and that he was never sure if he had learned from his father or if it were instinctual; he had, out of necessity, developed a quick-witted tongue, the result of being a younger brother to an even wittier sister, Amara, who he loved and admired very much. He was a quarter of an inch short of six-foot, dark skinned with a red tint, and almond shaped eyes colored black like a cartoonÕs. He carried the name of his grandfather who had emigrated to America 70 yearÕs prior from Cape Verde. His loosely curled hair, which sometimes lay straight, he believed was the only feature that connected him to his maternal grandpa Ð a Puerto Rican immigrant who had left his mom as an infant.

Despite his mixed ancestry, LeonÕs life experience was typical of an African-American boy growing up in the new millennium. He was born and raised in a small town in the northern part of Oklahoma, where the only four racial distinctions that existed were white, black, Asian, and Mexican. There was little in empirical proof, both statistically and individually, that would have suggested Leon was destined for great things, other than the faith and encouragement of his parents, and the strict reverence for academic accomplishment that was fostered in his small, government provided home.

One hundred years had passed from the year F. Scott Fitzgerald was admitted to Princeton in 1913. Leon had read FitzgeraldÕs novel, This Side of Paradise, with little amusement and little interest Now, it was the summer before he was to head off to Old Nassau himself, and he decided to revisit FitzgeraldÕs rendition of his time at Princeton. This time around the novel took on a new life. The young egoistÓ

Leon was fascinated as he re-read Fitzgerals novle that summer. Leon had visitied Priceotn once before while tyouring colleges in the north east with his friend Hillary. Now, as he re-read the novel, the building and lanscoape took on new realism that they had hel before, and Leon read with the eagerness of a young child the night before Christmas, wondering as the possibilits and imagineation of the magical, best damn place on earth.

Leon had fallen in love with the idea of Priceton as a young boy. The summer before 6th grade, he atedned a summer camp in which their worked a counselor named James who had just completed high school. Leon admired James, because James was a a started on the Enid High Basketbbal team, and because LeonÕs sister was a cheerlelsader, Leon attended religiously.

 But LEons admiration for James was not souley because of his basketball achieve,tnts, Btu as he watched james that summer, he saw a young man who carried himself with distinguish. Something about his glwing confidence, friendly dememanor, boyish smile, and kinly nateuyt. It was obvious to him tah James was diffenrt, and Leaon couldnÕtfigure out why, but he was drawn to James.

 Eduardo build a relationship with james that summer, No t onely becausehe liked to play basketball and,and James was always organinzign a game for the campers, but james was also in charge of the reading room, which was open wfo quit reading during the hours form 2-3pm.

 Leon grew up with hi head stuck inside books. He preferred fiction to non-fiction. And loved stori of made of an fatasyey worlds. He preferred the pop-wrtting of Lemony Snicket, Red Wall, and JK rowling to the clasisces that his high school English teachers would make him read. Excpet for shaespera. LEaon loved shakespear. Not just for the illustrious writin, but for the tragic stories that accomnaied. Leaon did not like stories with happy endings, this is probably whiy A series of Unfortuante events was his favrotu series growing up. Books with appy endings were, predictable. He felt they gave an unrealistic depiction of life. Fantssy words that were propgoated by marketers such as Walt Disney.

 One day inth reading room, James was sitting at a computer and Eduarod sat in th corner with ah bok and hand starring at James screen, something he felt he knew was an beeehc of pivacy, but ultimatey he didnÕt care. He watched as james went to s awebstoe that he had never seen, but that he was sure was age restricted. IN those days, communites were heavily policed online in odrder to protect and save face and appeareace ato give faith for worreisome mothers and fathers.

 As james loged on, leon watched as he scrolled down a feed of pictures, and he could see that james would stope periodically to look at who was in the picture. James paused for a lag time ona picture that was familiar to Leon. Julia. It was a photo of the famle lifeguard who worked at the pool that the campers would go to once, sometimes twice a week. Julia was by far the prettiest of all the lifeguards who worked at the pool, and LEons keen ssesne of awareness, even st such a young age, he picked up on the admiration that James had for Julia. And he was pretty certain Julia really liked James too, despite having a boyfriend.

 Leon creeped up slowly behind james. And watched as james commented something on the picture. ÒWay are you doingÓ he asked. Òjames quicly exited out of the screen before turning around, his face a little red as if I had caught him doing something he wasnÕt suppose to. Òwhat was that website.Ó Leon Asked. Òumm its this sight called facebook.Ó What is facebbok?Ó itÕs a website for college stufdnts, where they can connect with their classmates and other college students online.Ó SO you have to be in college to get a facebbokÓ Leon was disappointed, a little bit because he wanted to see more phots of Julia, as he was sure James did too just moments before. Òyes you have to be in college.Ó Well how do they know if im in collge or not, leaon replied. CouldnÕt I just lie about my age. Yes you could in theory james responddd. But they require you use a .edu email addreesss. Youll only have one of those if you are in college.

 Leon looked sulkingly back at the comuter screen that james had loged out of. Now the screen was on a login page with a username and password box that was blank. The username had JameÕs email address typed into still. And leon looked at the .edu that ended as thgoth to himself how much he couldnÕt wait to go to college. Then he noticed something else. The word Princeton came right before the .edu, and Leoan becae excited. You go to PRicneton?! He asked with enthusiasm. James had just been accepted to Nassau ealier that year. Leaon spent more of that summer getting to know and learn from jmes. And when james left for college, Leaon and he exchanged mailing addresses, and James kept in conteact with Leon ofr his first year ar PTicnon and every tyear after that. Leon wanted to attend princeotn, just like james.

His senior year of high school Leon applied Òealy actionÓ to Princeton. This was the first year in over 20 years that priceotn offerend early action, which was a way to apply early to unicersityes in order to show your commitemetn to the university, in hopes that they will take that into account in their admission decision. items.body_excerpt: The possibility to be anonymous or pseudonymous relies on you not revealing any identifying information about yourself in connection with the bitcoin addresses you use. If you post your bitcoin address on the web, then you’re associating that address and any transactions with it with the name you posted under. If you posted under a handle that you haven’t associated with your real identity, then you’re still pseudonymous.

 "hex": "hex-code#RRGGBB",
 "msg": "msg"
}

Key Required? Description
*p Yes Protocol: Helps other systems identify and process colour events
*op Yes Operation: Type of event (DID, put, remove, mix)
*hex Yes Hex-code of the exact colour/shade
*msg No any msg associated with the colour

NOTE: whoever owns the "put" inscription of a hex colour/shade owns it
